                What is happening. The tests show very low concern for the heart. This is most probably a panic attack.

                What was checked.

                What may be felt. Drowsy, heavy and a little foggy. In zero gravity it can feel extra floaty or slightly dizzy. Coordination and reaction time are slow for a few hours: do not touch switches or read checklists, and stay tethered.

                Post-therapy plan (draft for the physician)

                • Send the full summary to Earth and plan the return to definitive care. NASA's acute coronary syndrome form assigns removal to definitive care to every case.
                • Medicines to consider only if heart rate and pressure allow: metoprolol XL 50 mg tablet and lisinopril 10 mg tablet, and aspirin 325 mg once a day. All three are on the ISS medication list. The physician confirms.
                • Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under the tongue if chest pain returns, with the same holds as before.
                • Oxygen only if saturation is below 94%.
                • Monitor for 24 hours: ECG every 2 minutes at first and then hourly, repeat troponin and ultrasound, rest, no exercise.
                • Breathing protocol, and a crewmate stays beside the astronaut.

                Then, a short tour

                How it works in one line: ASCIS watches an astronaut's vital signs, compares them with that astronaut's own baseline, and guides the crew step by step when something changes. Everything here is simulated.

                The tabs at the top

                • Pre-flight: this screen: the astronaut's baselines, patient file and kit, plus a short tour. Open it any time.
                • Monitor: the live health screen and the demo buttons.
                • Earth: Mission Control's holographic screen. It opens in a new tab and follows the monitor live.
                • Eye check: a 30-second vision game, compared with your own baseline.
                • Play: two learning games.
                • Videos: short story videos, each solving one medical problem of space travel, sorted by NASA's five hazards.

                How to read the vitals

                • The big number is the live value. The badge says In your range, Raised or Low.
                • The colored bar is the astronaut's own range, not a textbook one. The marker shows where they are now.
                • "Signal good" or "Some motion noise" says how far to trust the number.
                • Ranges shift in space: blood pressure runs about 8 to 10 mmHg lower in orbit and resting temperature about 1 °C higher.

                Two-minute path

                1. Turn the voice on. Press "Voice: off" at the top. Browsers need one click before they can speak.
                2. At every step, press "Show reasoning" in the big assessment box. It explains why ASCIS decided: the signal check, the triggers, the risk index, the tests, the consent basis, and the ship inventory: every treatment subtracts supplies from a local counter, and low supplies are queued for Earth.
                3. Go to the Demo controls at the bottom of the Monitor. Press Subtle ECG change. ASCIS checks the signal, asks plain questions (answer as Crewmate B, the emergency proxy), runs tests, and offers aspirin.
                4. Press CO₂ rising: several signals fall together, and it stops at the aspirin. Then ST elevation, a known heart attack: watch the pump countdown (STOP or Confirm) and the evacuation plan.
                5. Press Cardiac arrest: the CPR device counts down, a soft chime sounds (you can silence it), and the vitals return.
                6. Press Panic at rest: the tests show low concern for the heart, so ASCIS asks about a calming medicine (Ativan) and breathes with the astronaut until they feel better. It never treats a fast heart as harmless without checking.
                7. Tap an organ dot on the body, try Day / Night, then open Earth in its own tab (keep both open and press a scenario here: Earth follows it), try Eye check, and open Play and Videos.

                Labels that say SI-generated mean made with synthetic intelligence (SI), also called AI: 3D models and pictures by Meshy, story videos by Canva, and code and text with Claude. Characters, scripts and medical content are our team's.

                Safe mode: simple limits and a checklist

                If the advanced analysis or a sensor fails, ASCIS keeps working with simple limits on the numbers that still work. This is a simulated failure. Draft for physician review.

                Paper and voice checklist

                1. Stop activity and attach to the web. Sit or lie still.
                2. Check breathing and pulse by hand. Count the pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
                3. Call the crew and Earth. Say the time and what you see.
                4. No pulse or not breathing: start CPR and use the AED.
                5. Use the paper medicine card. Never give a medicine without a second person confirming.
                6. Write down every action with its time.

                Saved black-box log

                  Guided neck-vein ultrasound (simulated)

                  Draft for physician review. Earth's radiologists can watch the live picture, with the delay.

                  1. Get ready. Sit upright or lie with the head slightly raised. Put gel on the left side of the neck.
                  2. Find the vein. Place the probe just beside the pulsing carotid artery. The internal jugular vein is the larger, softer circle next to it.
                  3. Press gently (the compression test). A healthy vein collapses completely. A vein with a clot stays open.
                  4. Look at the flow in color mode. Breathing should change the size of the vein. Slow, absent or reversed flow matters: NASA's working group names slow flow in this vein as the main clot risk.
                  5. Save the pictures and send them to Earth. Repeat the scan to confirm. In NASA's first case, a repeat scan confirmed the clot.

                  Tick everything that applies

                  How does space radiation affect astronauts?

                  Space is full of invisible particles that carry a lot of energy. When they pass through the body, they can damage cells and DNA.

                  Where it comes from

                  • Galactic cosmic rays from far outside our solar system.
                  • Solar particles thrown out by the Sun in a solar storm (a solar particle event).
                  • Trapped particles caught in Earth's magnetic belts, which a spacecraft passes through on its way.

                  What it can do to the body

                  • Over the long term: a higher chance of cancer, cataracts (a clouded eye lens), and damage to the heart and blood vessels. Effects on the brain and nerves are also being studied, and scientists are still learning how big that risk is.
                  • Right away: sickness is not expected, except after a very large solar storm that gives a high dose in a short time.

                  How it is measured

                  The unit is the sievert (Sv). One millisievert (mSv) is a thousandth of that. It counts the type of radiation and which organs are hit. The Radiation dose so far card shows an example: 41.2 mSv used of a 120 mSv demo budget, which is not an official limit. The National Academies recommended a career limit of 600 mSv, chosen to keep the extra risk of dying from cancer at or below 3%. On the real station, NASA's radiation team watches the levels around the clock.

                  Why it matters more far from Earth

                  Near Earth, the planet's magnetic field shields part of it. In deep space, astronauts lose that shield and face the full cosmic rays and solar particles.

                  The physics check

                  IdeaMathResult
                  Stopping a storm protonRange in water ≈ 0.0022 × E1.77 cm (E in MeV)A 100 MeV proton stops in about 7.6 cm of water, and a 200 MeV proton in about 26 cm. Water is rich in hydrogen, which stops protons well, so it is a favorite shielding material.
                  Warning timeLight from the Sun: 499 s. A 100 MeV proton moves at 0.43 c, so 499 ÷ 0.43Light arrives in about 8 minutes. Even in a straight line, those protons need about 19 minutes (longer in practice). That gap is the time for a warning.
                  Our example doseMission day 94 × about 0.44 mSv per dayAbout 41 mSv, the number on the dose card. It is an example, not a measurement.

                  What ASCIS does

                  • Shows the dose card, and flags a radiation reading above range in the reasoning panel.
                  • The Solar storm switch raises the reading, so you can watch ASCIS react.
                  • The Eye check logs extra white flashes, which cosmic rays can cause, and queues the note for Earth.
                  • ASCIS does not shield anyone. The crew follows flight rules and moves to the best-shielded area.

                  Sources: Canadian Space Agency, "How does radiation affect the human body in space?"; NASA Space Radiation Analysis Group, "Space Radiation: An Important Concern for Human Spaceflight"; National Research Council (2012), Technical Evaluation of the NASA Model for Cancer Risk to Astronauts Due to Space Radiation; National Academies recommendation of a 600 mSv career limit (2021); proton ranges from standard stopping-power tables. All dose numbers in the demo are simulated.

                  Eye check: a 30-second game

                  Your eyes are sensors too. In space, fluid shifts toward the head and can flatten the back of the eye, so near words may blur. Cosmic rays can also make tiny white flashes. ASCIS compares today with your own baseline. Everything here is simulated.

                  ⭐ 0 / 2 stars

                  Level 1: Read the line

                  Hold the screen at reading distance. Tap the smallest line you can read clearly. Your usual best is line 6.

                  Level 2: Count the sparkles

                  Rest in the dark for 10 minutes with your eyes closed. Tap + each time you see a white flash. Your usual: 3 flashes.

                  0

                  A screening game, not a diagnosis. Each reading line is about 0.25 D (diopters, a unit of lens power) in this demo. Urgent: a sudden dark curtain or shadow, sudden loss of vision, or eye pain. Contact Earth right away.

                  Play: two games

                  Game 1: Summit Trail

                  A learning game from ASCIS for two players (or one) that teaches astronauts to know their own numbers. It works offline, so it can teach even when the radio to Earth is silent. It has sound effects, and a Sound box switches them off.

                  How to play

                  1. Two players take turns, Player 1 first. Switch off "Two players" to play alone.
                  2. On your turn press Roll the dice. Your token climbs square by square from 1 toward the summit at 100.
                  3. Land on the bottom of a ladder to climb: a good reading or habit lifts you up.
                  4. Land on the head of a snake to slide down: a missed warning or a risky habit costs ground.
                  5. After each ladder or snake, read the short message. It teaches one habit.
                  6. You need an exact roll to land on 100. The first player to land on it wins a scratch card with their name on it: scratch it to reveal a treat.
                  7. Hover over or tap any square to read a short fact about it.
                  8. Reset board starts again.

                  Good to know

                  Nothing is saved. You can also reach it from the organ cards on the body: tap an organ and press "Play Summit Trail". The messages are drafts for physician review. The mountain picture is SI-generated.

                  Game 2: Find the Lost Star

                  A little star got lost in the dark. Solve three space first-aid riddles (a leaking suit, a broken arm, a toothache) to find her. At the end, two identical lights appear: use your science clues to tell the real star from burning space junk. Best for one player or a team, and it works offline.

                      Evacuation mode

                      Mission setting: space station. A return vehicle can bring the patient home in hours to days. Confirm the vehicle and the time window with Earth.

                      SI-generated concept (not built)

                      SI-generated 3D concept: a crew moving a patient on a stretcher. Not built.

                      Stabilization web (concept, not built). A tether from the astronaut’s bracelet to anchor points on the wall holds the patient and the helper still in microgravity. It steadies ultrasound scans and the ECG, supports CPR and makes moving the patient safer. The web is damped and stretchy and anchored to the station structure, so the patient’s momentum passes into the station, and it has a quick release for emergencies. Magnetic or mechanical anchors still need testing for interference with medical devices.

                      Draft for physician review. The destination and vehicle depend on the mission plan.

                      1. Decide with Earth. NASA’s acute coronary syndrome form assigns return to definitive care to every case. Confirm the vehicle and the time window. If there is no vehicle, treat in place and plan the return.
                      2. Stabilize first. Aspirin and the treating medicines are given and the vitals are stable before the move.
                      3. Secure the patient on the stretcher or the web, with the AED pads on.
                      4. Equipment pack: CPR device, AED, oxygen, IV line, the pump, the medical kit, and nitroglycerin with its holds.
                      5. Roles: the Commander decides, Crewmate B leads the patient, Crewmate C carries the equipment, Crewmate D prepares the route and contacts Earth.
                      6. During the move: ECG, oxygen and pressure stay on and the CPR device stays armed. If the heart stops, stop and start CPR.
                      7. On arrival: repeat the ECG, troponin and ultrasound, update Earth and continue the post-therapy plan.
                      8. Handover: send the black-box log and the medicine times.
